title: Circuit basics — simulate, build, and measure
description: Three hands-on lessons: voltage dividers, loading, and RC timing. Predict first, simulate an ideal circuit, then compare with a separate 3 V breadboard build.

schematics.title: Lesson 1 · Voltage divider
schematics.description: An ideal 3 V supply and two 1 kΩ series resistors. Inspect VOUT relative to GND.
assumptions: No external output load; ideal voltage probe

schematics.title: Lesson 2 · Loaded divider
schematics.description: The same divider with a 1 kΩ load from VOUT to GND. Compare with Lesson 1.
assumptions: R1 = R2 = RL = 1 kΩ, exact values
RL is in parallel with R2

schematics.title: Lesson 3 · RC charge and discharge
schematics.description: A slow 0–3 V square-wave source, 10 kΩ resistor, and 1000 µF capacitor. Time constant: 10 s.
assumptions: Ideal square wave: 0–3 V, 0.005 Hz, 50% duty cycle
R = 10 kΩ; C = 1000 µF; initial capacitor voltage = 0 V
No leakage, ESR, tolerance, or meter loading
Physical build uses manual input changes instead of a signal generator

STEP-001: Gather a breadboard, multimeter, switched two-AA holder, resistors and capacitor; expand Materials and bench setup in the tutorial.
Begin in simulation if parts are missing. Keep physical build and measurement milestones pending until actually performed.
Use the lesson navigation or Schematic selector below to browse. Field notes are separate for each lesson; repository roadmap progress changes only after a reviewed update.

tutorial.intro: A self-paced bench tutorial. Write a prediction before revealing answers. Keep predicted, simulated, and physically measured values separate; share each lesson’s results through Field notes.
materials: Breadboard, jumper wires, digital multimeter, and a switched two-AA holder with two AA cells (about 3 V). Power is needed only for physical exercises.

Three 1 kΩ resistors, one 10 kΩ timing resistor, and another 10 kΩ resistor for initial capacitor discharge. Ordinary ¼ W parts are sufficient. Optional 2 kΩ and extra 10 kΩ resistors support variations.
One 1000 µF electrolytic capacitor rated at least 6.3 V, plus a timer. Check polarity. Other RC values work if you recalculate R × C and choose a timing interval you can measure.
Build these circuits separately from the microphone and speaker. Disconnect the supply before rewiring; use resistance/continuity mode only on unpowered, discharged circuits.
Voltage measurements use COM and V/Ω sockets, with the meter across two nodes. Current is inferred in these lessons. Never put a meter in current mode directly across a supply.

lessons.title: Voltage, resistance, and a divider
lessons.goal: Explain why two equal series resistors produce half the supply voltage, then check a real build.
lessons.diagramAlt: Three-volt supply feeds R1, 1 kilohm, into VOUT; R2, 1 kilohm, connects VOUT to ground. Measure VOUT relative to ground.
lessons.concept: Voltage is a difference between two nodes. Current is charge flow through a branch. Resistance relates them: V = I × R. Here R1 and R2 are in series, so the same current flows through both. VOUT is measured relative to GND, the battery negative terminal; GND does not mean earth ground.
predict: Before opening the answer, calculate total resistance, battery current, and VOUT for VIN = 3.0 V, R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 1 kΩ. Use I = VIN / (R1 + R2), then VOUT = I × R2.
Predict VOUT if R2 becomes 2 kΩ while R1 stays 1 kΩ. Write both predictions in Field notes.
simulate: The matching CircuitJS1 model is below this lesson. It starts paused. Press Run, then hover over each resistor and the VOUT probe to inspect voltage and current.
Double-click R2 (the lower resistor) and change its resistance to 2000 Ω. Compare with your prediction. Restore it to 1000 Ω for the physical baseline.
Save browser draft keeps edits locally. Reset to repository version restores the starting model. The separate starting-circuit download works even before the simulator loads.
build: Use a breadboard and a switched two-AA holder, about 3 V. Disconnect the holder before wiring. Identify breadboard connected groups and any split power rails with the meter in continuity mode while unpowered.

With resistors separate from the circuit, measure R1 and R2 in resistance mode and record their actual values. Then connect battery + → R1 → VOUT → R2 → battery −. The junction must be a separate breadboard node from both supply rails.
Put the black meter lead in COM and red in V/Ω. Select DC volts before connecting power. This lesson infers current from voltage and resistance; leave the current-input socket unused.
measure: Power the circuit. Keep the black probe at battery − / GND. Measure VIN at battery +, then VOUT at the R1/R2 junction. Write the node pair, meter mode, and units with each reading.
Recalculate VOUT = measured VIN × measured R2 / (measured R1 + measured R2). Compare that prediction with the measured voltage and the ideal simulation.
Infer series current from (VIN − VOUT) / R1 and independently from VOUT / R2. Explain why the two estimates should be close. Disconnect power when finished.
expected: Ideal baseline: total resistance 2 kΩ, current 1.5 mA, VOUT 1.5 V. Each resistor dissipates 2.25 mW.
With R2 = 2 kΩ: total resistance 3 kΩ, current 1.0 mA, VOUT 2.0 V. A divider sets a ratio; it is not a fixed-voltage regulator.
Your AA voltage and resistor values will differ from the nominal model. A voltmeter also loads the circuit slightly. Treat this list as predictions, not completed measurements.
troubleshoot: VOUT near VIN or 0 V: disconnect power and check whether the junction shares a breadboard strip with a rail, or one resistor is not connected.
Unexpected ratio: measure resistors separately with power disconnected. In-circuit resistance includes other paths and is not necessarily the part value.
Negative voltage: check which node has the black probe. The sign depends on probe order.
lessons.transfer: Connection to the microphone project: a node name or connector polarity label does not tell you its voltage relative to ground. Record the reference node explicitly.

lessons.title: A measurement or load changes the circuit
lessons.goal: Predict how a connected load pulls down the divider output, then measure the change.
lessons.diagramAlt: Three-volt supply feeds R1, 1 kilohm, into VOUT. R2 and load RL, each 1 kilohm, both connect VOUT to ground in parallel.
lessons.concept: The load RL shares both endpoints with R2, so they are in parallel. Their equivalent resistance is Rbottom = (R2 × RL) / (R2 + RL). The divider becomes VOUT = VIN × Rbottom / (R1 + Rbottom). Connecting another device can change the signal you intended to observe.
predict: Use R1 = R2 = RL = 1 kΩ and VIN = 3.0 V. Calculate Rbottom, VOUT, current through R1, and current through each lower branch.
Predict whether a 10 kΩ load disturbs the original 1.5 V output more or less than a 1 kΩ load.
simulate: Run the loaded-divider model below. R1 is the upper resistor, R2 the lower center resistor, and RL the resistor to the right. Inspect the VOUT probe and compare branch currents.
Change RL from 1000 Ω to 10000 Ω, then 1000000 Ω. Observe how VOUT approaches the unloaded value as load resistance increases.
Restore RL = 1000 Ω before comparing the nominal model with your first physical load test.
build: Rebuild or retain the first lesson’s 1 kΩ / 1 kΩ divider. Disconnect power before adding the load.
Measure a third 1 kΩ resistor separately, then connect it from VOUT to GND. Both R2 and RL must share the same two nodes; do not insert RL in series with R2.
Keep meter leads in COM and V/Ω and select DC volts. You only need voltage and separate, unpowered resistance measurements.
measure: Measure VIN and VOUT with RL installed. Disconnect power, remove RL, reconnect power, and measure VIN and VOUT again. Record both conditions.
Use actual resistance readings to predict loaded VOUT. Infer IR1 = (VIN − VOUT) / R1, IR2 = VOUT / R2, and IRL = VOUT / RL. Check that IR1 approximately equals IR2 + IRL.
If you have a 10 kΩ resistor, repeat with that load and compare. Explain why a signal can appear correct until another device is connected. Disconnect power afterward.
expected: With a 1 kΩ load: Rbottom = 500 Ω; VOUT = 1.0 V; IR1 = 2.0 mA; IR2 = IRL = 1.0 mA.
With a 10 kΩ load: Rbottom ≈ 909 Ω and VOUT ≈ 1.429 V. With a 1 MΩ load: VOUT ≈ 1.499 V.
A typical high-input-resistance voltmeter is a much lighter load than 1 kΩ; check your meter’s specification rather than assuming its input resistance.
troubleshoot: VOUT increases after adding the load: check whether you accidentally changed the series path instead of connecting RL in parallel.
No visible change: verify RL is actually connected to both VOUT and GND, and that it is 1 kΩ rather than 1 MΩ.
Different supply readings between tests: use each test’s measured VIN in its own prediction.
lessons.transfer: Connection to the microphone project: an audio tap and an AUX input are electrical loads. We must characterize the source and plan buffering or conditioning before connecting them.

lessons.title: Capacitors take time: the RC response
lessons.goal: Measure a slow capacitor charge and discharge, and relate the shape to the time constant R × C.
lessons.diagramAlt: An input switching between zero and three volts feeds a 10-kilohm resistor into VC. A 1000-microfarad capacitor connects VC to ground with positive terminal at VC.
lessons.concept: A capacitor stores charge, Q = C × V. Charging current falls as its voltage approaches the supply. For an initially discharged capacitor and an ideal step to VIN, VC(t) = VIN × (1 − exp(−t/τ)), where τ = R × C. This circuit is a low-pass example: its output cannot follow fast input changes immediately.
predict: For R = 10 kΩ and C = 1000 µF, calculate τ. Predict VC after one, three, and five time constants with a 3.0 V input.
Predict what doubling R or C does to charging time. Predict the final voltage if the ideal input stays at 3.0 V.
simulate: The model below uses a square-wave input from 0 to 3 V at 0.005 Hz: 100 simulated seconds high, then 100 low. It uses a 10 kΩ resistor and an ideal 1000 µF capacitor, initially at 0 V.

Press Run and observe capacitor voltage in the scope. Use the simulator’s displayed time, not wall-clock time. The VC probe also shows node voltage. The falling input discharges the capacitor through the same resistor.

Change R to 20000 Ω and compare curve timing. Reset to repository version to return to the original values and initial condition. The ideal capacitor has no leakage, tolerance, or polarity failure model.
build: Disconnect the two-AA supply. Use R = 10 kΩ and C = 1000 µF, rated at least 6.3 V. Measure the resistor separately first. Read the capacitor marking; if a different capacitance is used, recalculate τ before testing.

Connect R from the input wire to VC. Connect capacitor + to VC and capacitor − to GND. An electrolytic’s stripe usually marks −; verify its markings. Battery − goes to GND. Leave the R input wire disconnected initially.

With the supply disconnected, place a separate 10 kΩ resistor across the capacitor for at least five time constants, then verify VC is below about 0.05 V in DC-voltage mode. Remove that discharge resistor before charging.
measure: Place the voltmeter across the capacitor: red at VC, black at GND. Measure and record the supply voltage first. Connect the R input wire to battery + and start a timer. Record VC near 10, 30, and 50 seconds, including actual elapsed times.

For discharge, disconnect the R input wire from battery + first, then connect that same wire to GND. Never connect battery + directly to GND. The capacitor now discharges through R. Record VC near 10, 30, and 50 seconds after this change.

Compare the measured curve with the ideal prediction using actual VIN and R. Roughly estimate τ as the charge time to 63% of VIN or the discharge time to 37% of its starting voltage. Account for capacitor tolerance, leakage, meter loading, and sampling delay.

Finish with the supply disconnected, discharge through the resistor, and check the remaining voltage. If no suitable capacitor is available, complete the simulation and leave the physical measurement explicitly pending.
expected: τ = 10000 Ω × 0.001 F = 10 s. At 10 s: VC ≈ 1.90 V; at 30 s: ≈ 2.85 V; at 50 s: ≈ 2.98 V for a 3.0 V step from zero.
For discharge starting at exactly 3.0 V, VC(t) = 3.0 × exp(−t/10 s): about 1.10 V at 10 s, 0.149 V at 30 s, and 0.020 V at 50 s. Scale these by your actual starting voltage.
Doubling R or C doubles τ. The ideal steady-state charge voltage stays at VIN. Real capacitor leakage and meter input resistance can lower the final measured value.
troubleshoot: Charging appears instantaneous: check the capacitance unit (1000 µF = 0.001 F), resistor value, and whether the resistor was bypassed by a shared breadboard strip.
Voltage stays near zero: disconnect power and verify the discharge resistor was removed, the input reaches R, and VC is not on the ground strip.

Voltage settles low or timing differs: verify polarity with power removed; measure actual VIN and R; consider capacitor tolerance, leakage, and the meter’s finite input resistance. Do not relabel an unexplained result as a confirmed component value.
lessons.transfer: Connection to the microphone project: this teaches RC behavior, but it is not a model of the microphone front end. A series coupling capacitor is a different topology and needs its own source, load, and bias analysis.
